body_markdown:
After it served tens of thousands of passengers and racked up years of highway miles, this aluminum-sided 1950s hauler was converted into a stylish RV. Now finished in birdseye maple and walnut throughout, it offers its passengers a dinette, a private bedroom in the back, and a compact bathroom.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


This RV started life as a 1955 Flxible VistaLiner VL-100. It’s reported to be one of just 220 built, and one of 10 still on the road. It was initially built for intercity[bus](https://www.hagerty.com/media/member-stories/this-46-chevy-is-the-coolest-bus-on-the-block/) routes, where its split-level design gave passengers up top a great view through the generous windows that wrapped up its sides and over its roof. The riders’ luggage, meanwhile, was secured in the ample storage area below. That same layout works just as well as an[RV](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/a-gmc-motor-homecoming-50-years-on/) : storage below leaves plenty of room for outdoor gear, and the highways supply an ever-changing landscape for the passengers.


While it was already meant for highway travel, the original powertrain was upgraded for even more pushing power. The bus is now motivated by a turbocharged 6V-92 Detroit Diesel and Allison four-speed automatic transmission. The Series 92 engines displace 92 cubic inches per cylinder and are a newer, larger version of the long-lived Series 71 engines that would have powered the bus when it was new. Like the Series 71 it was based on, these big two-strokes rely on a positive displacement blower to fill the cylinders, with more powerful variants adding a turbocharger and sometimes, as is the case in this example, a charge-air cooler. The 552-cubic-inch V-6 is rated at 350 horsepower and received a rebuild a few years ago at Central Truck Service in East Bethel, Minnesota.


Once parked, the on-board electricity is handed over to a 10-kW Yanmar diesel generator. It provides enough power to keep the refrigerator and air conditioner humming. If the site has access to power, the RV is ready for that as well, with 50-amp wiring ready for shore power.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


We asked Hagerty contributor and vintage bus aficionado Evan McCausland about this conversion. “Unlike many of its rivals, Flxible often sold incomplete intercity coaches—essentially rolling empty shells—for the purpose of having a third-party upfit the coach into a mobile office or motor coach,” said McCausland. “Custom Coach out of Columbus, Ohio, was a big name in this field. Obviously, this particular coach wasn’t such a conversion, but the transformation from motorcoach to motorhome still seems extremely well executed, which isn’t always the case. Finding something that was well-built in the first place and then actually used and properly maintained throughout its life is more difficult than you might think.” There are lots of fans of these vintage machines out there, helping keep them on the road. “I do think this would be a great addition and incredibly welcome at the Flxible Owners’ semi-annual homecoming event, wherein coaches return to Loudonville, Ohio, where they were originally manufactured,” added McCausland.


This 1950s highway hauler is currently up for sale on[Hagerty Marketplace](https://www.hagerty.com/marketplace/auction/1955-Flxible-VistaLiner/47ab28ba-44db-43e7-ac8a-0a5c15b8bb84) , where there are more photos and videos of its big diesel rumbling to life. Modern motorcoaches can offer impressive luxury and performance, but will they ever be as stunning as this polished aluminum people-mover? This might be the perfect motor coach for a small family looking to live large on the interstate.
